articles.body_html:
Word Press was released in the fantastic world of 2003, before 5G, wifi-7, and meta glasses.

I have been seeing Word Press everywhere the last few years. So many highlights of what people are doing with it, so many people wanting it managed. I wondered to myself if Word Press was something I needed to learn to make myself more marketable. Since I have actively avoided it, I wondered what exactly I was missing out on.

Investigation

A surface level investigation reveals that Word Press is a frequent target for bad guys, ( I refuse to say hacker because I want to remove the stigma that all hacking is bad. ) and you would have to pay special attention to patches, updates, and backups along with app hardening. Ignoring an update leaves you open to bugs or exploits. Complex customizations can make updating risky. Conflicts, bloat, and lack of optimization can slow you down. I don't think I need to continue, there is a lot of uncertainty.

Not sure if I'm interested in joining that party. So, THIS is why I see all of these Word Press jobs available. It all makes sense now. 😂

When I was first starting in web development, I would read all these Word Press memes and general complaints. It gave me a cringe feeling. To make matters worse, it seemed like every other available position was managing Word Press. Come oooooonnn dude. You want me to optimize on top of someone else lack of care? Hmm. No. Hire a developer. We need jobs! Let us build you something far more elegant, custom, and up to date. All we ask for in return is job security, no? 😂😂😂

Word Press may single handedly lead to the rise of the junior developer once again. 🤣 🥳 I’m not going to waste my time learning an over-bloated system with high security risks. I’ve got enough drama in my life. Personally? Knowing what I know now, I would not run the risk of putting my personal ecommerce site on Word Press. The bigger you are and the more you buy into, the more you expose yourself. I'm probably severing any possibility of ever working with Word Press here. Oh wellsies.

It’s better to stay as O.G. and annoyingly granular as possible. It’s more secure. It gives you pride. It gives you control, if you can accept responsibility for yourself and others. That's not to say there isn't use cases for using prebuilt tools and templates, there are. But I digress.

If security is not a valid concern for your use case, like in the case of a static website or recipe archive of some sort, than by all means, Word Press away! I’m sure this is perfect for some applications.

Here is a source of entertaining Word Press memes: https://www.wpfixit.com/wordpress-memes/

From my brief digging this morning, I've learned that Word Press is a fertile land of plugin chaos. 🦄 I will continue building fully functional features on my website from scratch, as I want to keep a thin slice of sanity. Leave it to a developer to complain about Word Press, of course. I guess it was my turn. 🤣

For Mr. Fancy Businessman

Hire a developer Mr. Fancy Businessman, that Junior developer will take you far further in the way that you prefer than Word Press likely ever could. Especially if you have anything of a unique situation. If the “bad guys” don’t understand your system architecture, you become more of a pain in the *ss to exploit. You bullet proof yourself to a degree. Be annoying and let them go for low hanging fruit elsewhere.

To My Peers

And to my peers: Don’t get overly reliant on AI. Go build a system at home, on a small computer, on a Linux device. Learn how to host it all and make it secure on your own network. Be a powerful developer, make the people that came before you proud. No laziness. If you want a junior role you must outshine the current capabilities of existing systems. That’s going to be a lot of work. Start now. (Or make your own business!)

Now, I am not completely dense. I only have an outsider perspective. What can you tell me about the ins and outs of Word Press land? I challenge you to slant my opinion. I am genuinely curious if for nothing else than entertainment value.

articles.title: Claude Code Output Validation Hooks in 2026: Linting Agent-Written Code Before It Touches Your Repo
articles.description: Deterministic validation hooks for AI-generated code. Stop type errors, security holes, and test failures before Claude commits them to your repository.
articles.body_html:
Claude Code Output Validation Hooks in 2026: Linting Agent-Written Code Before It Touches Your Repo

This article was written with the assistance of AI, under human supervision and review.

AI code agents produce output at a pace that makes manual review impractical. A Claude Code session can edit fifty files before the first test runs. The code lands in the repository clean or broken depending on whether validation happened before the commit. Most teams discover this after the damage shows up in CI.

The problem sits between the agent's tool execution and the repository state. Claude writes code that passes its internal checks but fails the toolchain's stricter rules. Type errors appear that TypeScript would have caught. Tests break that were passing ten minutes earlier. Security scanners flag patterns that a pre-commit hook would have blocked.

Claude Code workflow without validation showing compiler staying silent until CI fails

Validation hooks solve this by running checks at deterministic points in the agent's execution flow. A PreToolUse hook blocks a dangerous shell command before it runs. A PostToolUse hook lints every file edit and sends errors back to Claude for correction. A Stop hook verifies that tests pass before the turn ends.

Claude Code workflow with validation hooks showing checks passing before code reaches the repository

The validation happens in the same environment that runs the code. The agent sees the exact error message the compiler produces and fixes it in the next turn. The repository receives only code that already passed the checks.

Key Takeaways

  • Validation hooks intercept AI tool calls at specific execution points (before, after, or on session events) and run deterministic checks that return pass/fail decisions.
  • Exit code 2 blocks the action and returns stderr to Claude as feedback; exit 0 applies any JSON output fields but does not auto-approve.
  • PostToolUse hooks with formatters and linters are the most widely adopted pattern because they fix trivial errors automatically.
  • Agent-type hooks spawn subagents that can read files and run commands to verify conditions that require inspecting actual state rather than just evaluating input data.
  • Production workflows layer multiple hooks (linting, security scanning, test execution) with additionalContext injection to enforce repository policy deterministically.

PreToolUse vs PostToolUse: Choosing the Right Hook Point

Claude Code fires hook events at different stages of execution. The choice between PreToolUse and PostToolUse determines whether validation prevents an action or corrects it afterward.

A PreToolUse hook runs before the tool executes. The hook receives the tool name and input as JSON. Exiting with code 2 blocks the tool call and sends stderr back to Claude as the reason. This works for preventing destructive operations that cannot be undone.

Hook execution flow showing PreToolUse blocking risky operations and PostToolUse validating results

A PostToolUse hook runs after the tool finishes. The hook sees the tool output and can verify that the operation produced valid results. Exiting with code 2 here does not undo the tool call. Instead it signals that the output failed validation and Claude should try again.

The PreToolUse pattern prevents errors. The PostToolUse pattern detects and corrects them. Most production setups use both. Security checks run pre-execution to block dangerous patterns. Linters and formatters run post-execution to clean up style issues.

A Stop hook fires when Claude tries to end its turn. Exiting with code 2 sends Claude back to work with stderr as the reason it cannot finish yet. This enforces that work meets completion criteria before the turn ends.

The timing decision depends on what can be fixed automatically. Formatters and linters produce errors that Claude can resolve by re-editing the file. Those belong in PostToolUse hooks. Destructive operations like dropping database tables cannot be fixed after execution. Those require PreToolUse blocks.

Building a Pre-Commit Linting Hook That Blocks Bad Edits

The most effective validation hook runs TypeScript's compiler in --noEmit mode after every file edit. The hook exits with code 2 if type errors exist, which blocks the turn from ending and sends the full compiler output back to Claude.

Developers place this hook at .claude/settings.json in the repository root so it applies to every team member who works in the project, as documented at https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks. Workspace trust controls when the hook starts running on each machine.

{
  "hooks": {
    "Stop": [
      {
        "type": "command",
        "command": "pnpm tsc --noEmit 1>&2 || exit 2"
      }
    ]
  }
}

The 1>&2 redirection sends TypeScript's output to stderr because Claude Code reads stderr as the block reason when a hook exits with code 2. Without the redirect, the compiler errors go to stdout and Claude never sees them.

The hook runs every time Claude tries to stop. If the compiler finds errors, the exit code 2 prevents the turn from ending. Claude receives the type errors and continues working until tsc passes.

Claude Code validation hooks running TypeScript compiler checks

This pattern extends to any tool that reports errors on stderr and uses exit codes. ESLint with --max-warnings 0 blocks on linting violations. Prettier with --check blocks when formatting is inconsistent.

{
  "hooks": {
    "Stop": [
      {
        "type": "command",
        "command": "pnpm tsc --noEmit 1>&2 || exit 2"
      },
      {
        "type": "command",
        "command": "pnpm eslint . --max-warnings 0 1>&2 || exit 2"
      }
    ]
  }
}

Hooks in the same event array run in parallel. Both the typecheck and the linter execute at the same time. If either exits with code 2, the turn stays blocked until both pass.

The default block cap is eight consecutive stops with exit code 2 and no tool calls between them. After eight blocks, Claude Code overrides the next block and ends the turn anyway. Teams that need a higher cap set the CLAUDE_CODE_STOP_HOOK_BLOCK_CAP environment variable, documented at https://code.claude.com/docs/en/env-vars.

PostToolUse Feedback Loops: Teaching Claude to Fix Its Own Mistakes

PostToolUse hooks run after a tool finishes and receive the tool's output as part of the hook input. Exit code 2 in a PostToolUse hook does not block the original tool call because the tool already executed. Instead it signals that validation failed and Claude should continue the turn to address the errors.

PostToolUse feedback loop showing Claude editing, hook validating, and Claude fixing errors until validation passes

The hook script receives JSON on stdin that includes the tool name, input, and output. A PostToolUse hook for file edits parses this input to extract the edited file path and runs a linter against it.

#!/usr/bin/env node

const input = JSON.parse(require('fs').readFileSync(0, 'utf-8'));

if (input.tool_name === 'Write') {
  const filePath = input.tool_input.path;
  const { execSync } = require('child_process');

  try {
    execSync(`eslint ${filePath} --max-warnings 0`, {
      stdio: 'inherit',
      encoding: 'utf-8'
    });
  } catch (error) {
    process.stderr.write(`Linting failed for ${filePath}\n`);
    process.exit(2);
  }
}

process.exit(0);

The script checks whether the tool that just ran was Write. If so, it lints the file. A linting failure causes the script to exit with code 2 and write the error to stderr. Claude sees this feedback and edits the file again to fix the violations.

The feedback loop continues until the linter passes. Each iteration gives Claude the exact error message and line number. The agent applies the fix and the hook validates again. The turn ends only when no errors remain.

This pattern handles any validation that can be expressed as a deterministic check. Formatters, type checkers, and test runners all fit. The hook runs the check, and Claude iterates until it passes. The pattern works better than prompting Claude to "make sure to lint" because the hook enforces the requirement regardless of how Claude interprets the instruction.

Teams extend this approach to security scanning by running tools like semgrep or gitleaks in PostToolUse hooks. A finding triggers exit code 2 with the scanner's output on stderr. Claude sees which pattern triggered the alert and rewrites the code to avoid it.

Security Scanners and Test Runners as Validation Hooks

Security scanning belongs in PreToolUse hooks for shell commands and PostToolUse hooks for file edits. A PreToolUse hook on the Bash tool receives the command as part of the hook input and can block execution if the command matches a dangerous pattern.

{
  "hooks": {
    "PreToolUse": [
      {
        "type": "command",
        "command": "node .claude/hooks/security-check.js"
      }
    ]
  }
}

The security check script parses stdin to extract the command and matches it against a deny list.

#!/usr/bin/env node

const input = JSON.parse(require('fs').readFileSync(0, 'utf-8'));

if (input.tool_name === 'Bash') {
  const command = input.tool_input.command;
  const dangerous = [
    /rm\s+-rf\s+\//,
    /drop\s+table/i,
    /chmod\s+777/,
    /curl.*\|\s*bash/
  ];

  for (const pattern of dangerous) {
    if (pattern.test(command)) {
      process.stderr.write(
        `Blocked dangerous command: ${command}\n`
      );
      process.exit(2);
    }
  }
}

process.exit(0);

The hook exits with code 2 if the command matches any pattern. Claude receives the stderr message and knows the command was blocked. The agent adjusts its approach without executing the dangerous operation.

Test runners fit better in Stop hooks than in PostToolUse hooks because a single edit can break tests in unrelated files. Running tests after every file write creates unnecessary execution overhead. Running them once when Claude declares the work complete gives a single validation point.

{
  "hooks": {
    "Stop": [
      {
        "type": "command",
        "command": "pnpm test --run 1>&2 || exit 2",
        "timeout": 60
      }
    ]
  }
}

The timeout field gives the test suite 60 seconds to complete. If tests fail, the stderr output returns to Claude with the failure details. The agent reads which tests broke and continues the turn to fix them.

Security scanning and test execution as validation hooks

Some teams run focused test suites in PostToolUse hooks when an edit touches specific directories. A hook script checks the edited file path and runs only the related test file if one exists.

#!/usr/bin/env node

const input = JSON.parse(require('fs').readFileSync(0, 'utf-8'));

if (input.tool_name === 'Write') {
  const filePath = input.tool_input.path;
  const testPath = filePath.replace(/\.ts$/, '.test.ts');

  const fs = require('fs');
  if (fs.existsSync(testPath)) {
    const { execSync } = require('child_process');
    try {
      execSync(`pnpm test ${testPath} --run`, {
        stdio: 'inherit'
      });
    } catch (error) {
      process.stderr.write(`Tests failed for ${testPath}\n`);
      process.exit(2);
    }
  }
}

process.exit(0);

This approach gives fast feedback on test failures without running the entire suite after every edit. The full suite still runs in the Stop hook to catch cross-file regressions.

Command vs Prompt vs Agent Hook Types: When to Use Each

Claude Code supports three primary hook types that differ in how they make validation decisions. Command hooks run shell scripts, prompt hooks send a question to a Claude model for single-turn evaluation, and agent hooks spawn subagents that can use tools to investigate before deciding.

Comparison of command, prompt, and agent hook types showing execution patterns and decision mechanisms

Command hooks (type: "command") execute a shell command or script that receives the hook event data on stdin and communicates results through exit codes and stdout. The script has full access to the repository and can run any validation tool. This type handles most validation needs.

Prompt hooks (type: "prompt") send the hook input to a Claude model along with a prompt that asks for a decision. The model returns a JSON object with ok and reason fields. Prompt hooks work when the validation logic is too complex for a static script but does not require inspecting files. The official documentation at https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks shows examples of prompt hooks that evaluate whether a commit message follows conventional commit format.

Agent hooks (type: "agent") spawn a subagent that can use tools like Read, Grep, and Glob to verify conditions before returning a decision. The agent receives a prompt and the hook input, investigates using up to 50 tool turns, and returns a structured ok/reason response. This type fits verification that requires inspecting actual file contents or running commands to determine state.

Hook type Decision mechanism Filesystem access When to use
Command Exit code and stdout Direct shell access Deterministic checks with existing tools
Prompt Single LLM call returning JSON None, evaluates input data only Complex logic that does not need file inspection
Agent Subagent with tools over 50 turns Read, Grep, Glob tools Verification requiring actual codebase state

Command hooks cost nothing beyond the compute time to run the validation tool. Prompt hooks consume tokens on every invocation. Agent hooks can consume significant tokens if they perform extensive file reads or searches. The claude-code-cost-control-production post covers budgeting strategies for hook token usage.

Most teams start with command hooks for linting, typechecking, and security scanning. Prompt hooks enter the workflow when validation requires understanding intent rather than matching patterns. Agent hooks appear in workflows that need to verify cross-file consistency or check that tests exist for new features.

The official documentation at https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks describes agent hooks as experimental with behavior and configuration subject to change. Production workflows that require stability prefer command hooks with explicit tool invocations over agent hooks that may behave differently across Claude Code versions.

Production Validation Patterns: Multi-Stage Hooks and additionalContext

Production repositories layer multiple validation hooks that run at different execution points and inject context that guides Claude toward correct patterns. The layering creates defense in depth where each hook enforces a different aspect of repository policy.

Multi-stage validation flow showing security check, linting, testing, and context injection

A typical production configuration includes PreToolUse hooks that block dangerous operations, PostToolUse hooks that validate file edits, Stop hooks that enforce completion criteria, and SubagentStart hooks that inject security guidelines into background tasks.

The additionalContext field in hook output adds text to Claude's context. A SubagentStart hook can inject repository-specific rules that apply only when a subagent runs, as documented at https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks.

{
  "hooks": {
    "SubagentStart": [
      {
        "type": "command",
        "command": "node .claude/hooks/inject-security-context.js"
      }
    ]
  }
}

The injection script reads security guidelines from a file and returns them in the hookSpecificOutput field.

#!/usr/bin/env node

const fs = require('fs');
const guidelines = fs.readFileSync(
  '.claude/security-guidelines.md',
  'utf-8'
);

const output = {
  hookSpecificOutput: {
    hookEventName: 'SubagentStart',
    additionalContext: guidelines
  }
};

process.stdout.write(JSON.stringify(output));
process.exit(0);

The subagent receives these guidelines in its initial context before its first prompt. This pattern keeps security rules in a single source file that applies automatically to all subagent work.

Hook precedence determines which settings file wins when the same hook appears in multiple locations. Managed settings override project settings, which override user settings. The claude-code-structured-output-zod post covers settings precedence in detail.

Teams that enforce validation hooks organization-wide place them in managed settings files that individual repositories cannot override. A managed Stop hook that requires passing tests applies to every project regardless of local configuration.

Production teams set onFailure: "block" on critical hooks to ensure that hook failures prevent the action even when the hook exits with a non-standard error code. This field appears in the hook handler object alongside type and command.

{
  "hooks": {
    "PreToolUse": [
      {
        "type": "command",
        "command": "node .claude/hooks/security-check.js",
        "onFailure": "block"
      }
    ]
  }
}

With onFailure set to "block", a hook that crashes or times out blocks the tool call instead of allowing it through. This setting matters for security hooks where a failure to validate should err on the side of blocking rather than permitting.

The multi-stage pattern combines fast feedback from PostToolUse hooks with comprehensive validation from Stop hooks. Linters and formatters run immediately after edits so Claude sees errors while the file is still in working memory. The full test suite runs once at the end to catch cross-file issues.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can validation hooks slow down Claude Code sessions significantly?

Hooks add latency proportional to the validation tool's runtime. A TypeScript typecheck that takes five seconds blocks the turn for five seconds. Fast linters like ESLint add under one second. Hooks run in parallel when multiple handlers exist for the same event, so a typecheck and a linter running together take the time of the slower tool, not the sum. The timeout field limits how long Claude Code waits before considering the hook failed.

What happens when a hook exits with code 2 but prints valid JSON to stdout?

Claude Code reads the JSON fields even when the hook blocks with exit code 2. Decision fields like permissionDecision: "block" apply, but the block from the exit code stands regardless. The JSON can add a structured reason or inject context, but it cannot override the block. The official documentation at https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks includes a table showing which fields apply on each exit code.

Do hooks configured in a repository apply to every developer who clones it?

Hooks in .claude/settings.json apply to everyone who works in the project after they accept the workspace trust dialog for that folder. Deny rules apply immediately. Allow rules and hooks wait for trust acceptance. Each developer's local machine respects the CLAUDE_CODE_STOP_HOOK_BLOCK_CAP setting, so teams that need higher caps document the required environment variable in the repository README.

Can agent-type hooks access environment variables and credentials?

Agent hooks spawn subagents that run in the same environment as the main session. Environment variables available to Claude Code are visible to the subagent. Credentials stored in environment variables or accessible via the system's credential store work in agent hooks the same way they work in command hooks. The subagent's tool set determines what it can access, and agent definitions can restrict tools to Read, Grep, and Glob to prevent modification.

How do hooks interact with Claude's prompt cache to avoid redundant context loading?

SubagentStart hooks that inject additionalContext place that content in the subagent's context before its first prompt. Claude Code reuses this context across requests via prompt caching as documented at https://code.claude.com/docs/en/prompt-caching. When the subagent's context undergoes auto-compaction and discards the injected copy, the next SubagentStart hook run injects it again, maintaining the guideline presence without breaking the cache.

Making Validation Hooks Repository Policy

Validation hooks enforce what prompts and documentation only suggest. A CLAUDE.md file that says "always run tests" depends on Claude interpreting and following that instruction. A Stop hook that exits with code 2 when tests fail makes the requirement deterministic.

The shift from guidance to policy changes how teams use AI coding tools in production. Repositories with comprehensive hook coverage allow less experienced developers to work with Claude because the hooks prevent the common mistakes that would otherwise require senior review. The claude-code-ci-agentic-review-test-auto-fix post shows how validation hooks integrate with CI to create a complete quality gate.

Hooks belong in the repository's .claude/settings.json file where they version-control alongside the code. Teams that adopt hooks as policy commit them to the main branch and document them in the project README. Developers who join the project inherit the validation rules when they accept workspace trust for the repository.

Organizations that enforce hooks across all repositories place them in managed settings. The hooks run whether or not individual projects configure them locally. This approach makes security scanning and compliance checks organization-wide policy rather than per-project configuration.

Validation hooks turn AI code generation from a supervised activity into a governed process. The agent operates within deterministic boundaries that hold regardless of how it reasons about the task.

articles.body_html:
Let me tell you a story about a sandwich 🥪

Open the About page on DEV and you will find this sentence:

Ben ( @ben ) is the B. Peter ( @peter ) is the P. Jess ( @jess ) is the J. A peanut butter and jelly sandwich, made out of three people.

I read that line and had one of those "wait, how did this actually happen?" moments. I knew DEV started as a Twitter account. I knew it got big. I knew it was open source. But I had no idea how three people ended up running it together, who did what, or how the whole thing started in the first place.

So I went and read everything I could find. Podcast transcripts. AMAs. Old progress reports. Funding announcements. A college newspaper article from 2009 (yes, really). And what I found was a better story than I expected, with a missing date, a mystery typo, a Twitter account with 108,000 followers, and a plot twist in February 2026.

This post is that story, told in order, so you do not have to piece it together like I did.

The rules I am following


Before we start, a few promises, because this kind of article is easy to get wrong.
  • I did not talk to any of them. Everything here comes from things the founders and companies made public. When someone told a story about themselves, I say "Ben said" or "Jess wrote." I have not checked their personal stories against anyone else, and I say so when it matters.
  • When I am guessing, I will say "I am guessing." A few dates have to be worked out from other numbers. Those are marked as my math, not as official facts.
  • When nobody has said something, I will not invent it. There are real gaps, like deal prices and exact titles. I will point at the gap and move on.

Who is who (so you do not get lost)

Here is the cast, so you can come back to this if you get confused:

Ben Halpern started the Twitter account that became DEV. He is the funny one, the one who writes most of the announcements, and the one most people think of first.

Peter Kim Frank (sometimes just "Peter Frank") is Ben's earlier business partner. He is the one on the business side, and he has been running online projects since high school.

Jess Lee met Ben a bit later, joined the project in 2016, and runs operations. Jess uses they/them pronouns, which Jess shared in a post in March 2026, so that is what I use here. When I quote older interviews that say "she," I leave them as they were.

And two words people mix up constantly:

DEV is the community, the website at dev.to.

Forem is the open-source software DEV runs on (and the company that grew around it). DEV is the first Forem. We will get to why that matters.

Okay. Ready? Let's go back to the beginning. Or at least, as far back as the record goes.

Table of Contents

  • Chapter 1: A guy with a second Twitter account 🐦
  • Chapter 2: The business partner who started young
  • Chapter 3: The person who did not know what a startup was
  • Chapter 4: From a joke account to an actual website
  • Chapter 5: The decision, and the date that cannot be right 🕵️
  • Chapter 6: The year everything grew 17 times
  • Chapter 7: The day the code went public 🔓
  • Chapter 8: Money arrives, and the office disappears
  • Chapter 9: DEV gets a big sibling called Forem 🌍
  • Interlude: how DEV actually felt to run
  • Who does what, in plain English
  • Chapter 10: February 18, 2026 🚀
  • Where the three are now
  • Epilogue: the ten-year promise

Chapter 1: A guy with a second Twitter account 🐦

Our story starts with Ben, and Ben starts with a website he built at about 13.

In a Learn to Code With Me interview, Ben said he grew up fascinated with HTML and built websites as a hobby. His first real application, he told Developer Tea, was a fantasy sports site. He has also said he has been an entrepreneur in some form "since I was 12." (That one is from the Changelog interview.)

Then the plot gets less straight. He took some computer science in college, dropped out of that track, and graduated with a marketing degree. He interned somewhere and did not enjoy it. So he thought about comedy writing, spent a summer in New York living with his brother and trying to meet people in TV, and found there was not much of a path.

Meanwhile he had stopped believing programming was for him. A professor had discouraged him, and he has admitted to imposter syndrome. Then around 2012, a friend in a college cafeteria pointed him at Ruby on Rails while Ben was thinking about an app idea. That was it. He got back into programming "for real," he said, and he loved it.

He also overdid it. He has talked about 17 and 18 hour coding days, and about getting shingles twice from overwork. So when you read the rest of this story and think "these people worked a lot," keep that in mind. At least one of them has told you how much.

Where does the Twitter account come in?

Here is the part I like.

Ben's own profile says he is "a Canadian software developer who thinks he's funny." In his 2017 interview on Developer Tea, he explained that he made a second Twitter account, The Practical Dev, so he could post about programming without annoying the friends who followed his personal one.

Notice what that is. It is not a business plan. It is a guy trying not to spam his friends.

At first the account shared programming articles. Then he added his own opinions and jokes, and that is when it "really started taking off." He also said his marketing degree helped him understand how to grow it, so the degree he thought he wasted came in handy.

He told Learn to Code With Me that jokes are only about 5 percent of what the account posts. Which is funny, given what people remember it for.

The Changelog hosts asked him about the O'Reilly-style parody book covers. Ben called them "the first major chapter" of the story. If you have ever seen a fake programming book cover with an animal and an absurd title, that style of joke is part of what made the account spread.

When did this start?

Ben does not give a birthday for the account in the interviews I read. But the founders' first progress report, from November 2017, says it had been 1,174 days since the account started. If you count back from November 1, 2017, that lands around August 15, 2014.

That is my math, not an official date. I will do the same trick with other dates in a minute.

By April 2017, when Ben spoke to Developer Tea, the account had about 108,000 followers. In an earlier interview he said "just under 100,000." Each tweet, he said, sent a few thousand people to dev.to.

So hold that picture: a joke account, three years old, with a big and loyal audience, and a guy who has just realized the audience could be a community.

Right. Now meet the second person.

↑ Back to contents

Chapter 2: The business partner who started young

If you want to understand Peter, start with a college newspaper from 2009.

The Wesleyan Argus ran a story in February 2009 about a freshman in the class of 2012, Peter Frank, who was running a website called CollegeACB from his dorm room. ACB stands for anonymous confession board. It was a network of roughly 500 boards for different schools, and the Wesleyan one was the busiest.

Here is what the article says, and I am only repeating it:

  • CollegeACB had been started about a year earlier by two other students. Peter took it over about three months before the article, after they said they wanted a successor.
  • He had already been running a small company, Sumdae LLC, since his sophomore year of high school in 2005. It was built on registering domain names.

Chapter 4: From a joke account to an actual website

So how does a Twitter account turn into a website?

Slowly, and with a few accidents.

Ben told Developer Tea that he first registered practicaldev.com, and later switched to the shorter dev.to. According to the November 2017 progress report, the dev.to domain was bought about 550 days before the post, which lands around April 30, 2016. (My arithmetic again.)

Ben also said that around this time he decided to take the project seriously and build a real programming platform, while keeping most of his creativity pointed at the Twitter account. That sounds right to me. The account was the thing people loved, and the site had to earn its place next to it.

His goal, as he put it on the Changelog, was to fix the things he had been making fun of: career chaos, inconsistent learning resources, and a lack of tools and places for developers to gather. In other words, the jokes were the symptoms and the site was the treatment.

The first article was an interview with DHH

This is my favorite detail in the whole story.

Ben told the Changelog that the first thing published on dev.to was an interview with DHH, the creator of Rails, timed around the Rails 5 release. How did a guy with a joke account land an interview with one of the most famous names in the Ruby world? Ben said he emailed him, asked nicely, and made it easy to say yes. That is the whole trick.

He lined up more interviews with other open-source people after that. The original idea was a high-touch, interview-driven site. Then, he said, audience feedback pushed it in a different direction: a place where anyone could write about anything software-related, with an enforced code of conduct.

If you have used DEV, you know which version won.

The login button nobody could find

Here is a detail that made me laugh. Ben said the login feature was hidden in the footer at first. Hidden. And people found it anyway and logged in in large numbers, which surprised him.

A few other early choices are worth knowing, because they explain why DEV felt the way it did:

Sign-up needed an existing Twitter or GitHub account.

Ben called that a low barrier for most developers. It also gave the team some history to look at, since a brand new account that mirrors a banned one can be flagged as spam or harassment. If you had neither account, he said, they worked with you.

Writers could cross-post.

Jess said an early feature let creators import posts through RSS while keeping their canonical URL, so people could bring their blog posts with them without losing credit.

The team reached out to writers by hand.

And the Twitter account amplified quality content from writers who were not famous, which Jess says helped DEV grow.

The technical choices were deliberately dull.

Ben picked Rails and called it "boring and old" on the Changelog, which he meant as a compliment. In his 2021 Indie Hackers AMA, he said the choice of "solid, stable technology" was the best early decision they made. He also said he had been using Node at his day job and wanted an environment he liked more.

One more quote I like from Developer Tea:

Ben was making the case that a person explaining a tool in their own words is often more useful than the project's official docs. That is basically DEV's entire pitch in one sentence.

The worry that almost stopped it

Now for the quiet tension in this chapter.

Ben told the Changelog he was protective of the project. He worried that turning it into a business could ruin it. He wanted everything on the site to be "additive," not extractive.

What changed his mind? A conversation with Saron Yitbarek, the founder of CodeNewbie, who had just left her job to run CodeNewbie full-time. Seeing that, Ben said, helped him believe the project could be a real business.

And then he made a promise: he committed to giving the project ten years. In his 2021 Indie Hackers AMA, he repeated that as advice for anyone building open-source companies: commit to a ten-year horizon, even through the slow years.

Hold on to that ten-year promise. We will come back to it at the end.

How big was it, at the very start?

We have exactly one number from the early days, and it comes from the progress report. The team ended October 2016 with 69,259 sessions for the month.

That is not nothing, but it is small. A year later, the same report would say something very different. We will get there. First, we need to answer the question that has been hanging over this whole story.

How did three people become a company?

In the Dec 2017 AMA, he put it more simply: when dev.to "could be bigger than a two-person side project," that is when they brought Peter on. And, with a joke, he said, "Having three partners is great for breaking ties in arguments."

Wait. January 2016?

Here is where the detective work starts.

The progress report says the three agreed to combine "in January 2016." I read that line, then read the post's own numbers, and something did not add up.

Let me lay it out, because this is the kind of thing you can only trust if you can check it yourself:

  1. Jess had not joined yet in January 2016. By the report's day counts, Jess joined 485 days before November 1, 2017. That is about July 2016. So Jess could not have been preparing to go full-time six months before even starting.
  2. Ten months does not match 2016. The report says the merged team had been together for "about ten months." Ten months before November 2017 is roughly January 2017.
  3. The report says they were dreaming of it a year earlier. It also says that in October 2016 they were "dreaming of" working on dev.to full-time. That only makes sense if the decision came after October 2016.

So my reading is that "2016" is a typo for 2017. And I am fairly sure, because more sources lean the same way:

  • In the AMA Peter posted on December 20, 2017, he says he has worked on dev.to with Ben and Jess "since last January."
  • Peter's DEV profile says he joined on January 3, 2017.
  • In the same thread, Ben says they brought Peter on when dev.to "could be bigger than a two-person side project earlier this year." (Earlier this year, as in 2017.)
  • Jess, in the 2021 interview, says the team went full-time in 2017.

I want to be honest about what this is. It is an inference from the report's internal numbers and the founders' other statements. I did not find anyone correcting the original post. But I would be surprised if the answer were anything other than January 2017.

A coincidence I cannot explain

While I was working on this, I found something interesting. DEV has a Product Hunt page with a launch date of January 2, 2017. The ranking of number one for the day is credited to January 3.

So the Product Hunt launch, Peter's DEV join date, and the "January" decision all happen in the same few days.

I want to be very clear: I have no evidence that these are connected. It may just be a coincidence of timing. I also cannot fully explain why the page shows two dates for the launch. Time zones and the way Product Hunt displays launches might explain a one-day gap, but that is a guess, and the upvote counts on the page were ambiguous, so I am leaving them out. The founders do not say the launch caused anything. I will not say it for them.

What the report does not tell us

This is one of the places where the record goes quiet, so let me list what is missing, because it is a lot:

  • Who suggested the merger.
  • How equity was split, or what anyone was paid.
  • How titles were handed out.
  • Who came up with "PBJ" and why it stuck.

I looked for these elsewhere and found nothing. That does not mean the answers do not exist. It means they have not been made public, as far as I can tell.

One line from that thread keeps coming back to me, because it is a trade-off many founders would recognize. You "can't do any of this in an authoritarian way," he said, and you "have to frustrate some people in order to stick to your personal values." And on decentralization, he said it has to be made invisible through good UX, because most people move toward usable, delightful experiences.

What a "Forem" looked like in practice

Jess's 2021 interview gives some real-world examples.

  • Forem also powers the CodeNewbie Community.
  • Companies like Microsoft Azure and AWS now publish on DEV through organization accounts. Jess called that a "plan for opportunism" moment, a principle that guided their career.
  • New Relic launched "The Relicans" on Forem and chose the hosted version instead of self-hosting.
  • The company produces two podcasts: DevDiscuss (Jess and Ben) and DevNews (Saron Yitbarek and Josh Puetz).
  • Jess leads Nevertheless She Coded, a campaign tied to International Women's Day on March 8. In 2021 it was in its fifth year.

The one sentence that clears this up

So here is the simplest way to hold it in your head:


DEV is a place. Forem is the software that makes places like it.

DEV is the first and biggest Forem. When one source says "the co-founders of DEV" and another says "the co-founders of Forem," they mean the same three people at different points in the company's history.

And what happened to Forem as a business after 2021? I could not find reliable public numbers on customers, instance counts or revenue. So I will not make any up.

↑ Back to contents

Interlude: how DEV actually felt to run

Before the big news, let me step out of the timeline for a moment, because a few things the founders said explain why DEV felt different from other places. This is the "how," and it helps make the "what happened next" make sense.

The community was the point

When the Changelog hosts asked Ben for the secret sauce, he said it was merging "fundamental human community needs with practical software development needs." He described DEV as something like Medium for developers, with portfolio features like showing your GitHub projects, and, he said, no recruiter spam. Members could host posts on their own blogs and cross-post.

He told one small story that stuck with me. A member had shut down a language project he had worked on for years, and the community showed up to support him. That is not the kind of thing you plan for in a product spec.

Moderation, in their own words

DEV's approach to moderation comes up in almost every interview, so it is worth laying out.

Ben said DEV's main difference from Twitter was that it moderates at all. He called the platform pro free speech "in every way that's practical," but said other platforms are naive about human behavior and how some groups are more vulnerable than others. He also said Twitter did not treat harassment as a problem until the outside world called it out.

The tools he described:

  • A code of conduct that the team enforces.
  • Crowdsourced reports that can escalate quickly to admins.
  • Private messaging and small chat rooms that act as "break-out rooms" away from big public threads.
  • Account history checks, so a brand-new account mirroring a banned one can be flagged.

He also noted that harassment often arrives after a post gets shared on Hacker News or Reddit. And he said the team wrote down the DEV voice in documents, with guidance like "Say this, not this," because he handled most of the communication himself and the voice had to scale.

Jess described the same philosophy in 2021. Moderation should be values-driven and human-led, not outsourced, and people who cross the line get banned. A friendly, welcoming tone lowers the barrier for newer developers. And "repeat questions are totally valid," Jess said, because the answers change as technology changes.

That is how two founders describe it. I did not find an independent audit of how well it worked in practice.

The tech, kept boring on purpose

On the engineering side, Ben's description on the Changelog is a masterclass in not overcomplicating things.

  • About 90 percent of traffic is served from the CDN, he said, so most page loads do not touch Rails at all.
  • Pages are served without personal information. Anything specific to you loads in a quick asynchronous call and is cached in local storage.
  • The CDN is Fastly, and he praised its instant purge, with cache clears taking roughly 100 to 200 milliseconds.
  • Algolia handles search, so a user in a place like Tokyo gets fast responses from nearby nodes.
  • Ben described using Varnish Configuration Language on the edge, which is a less common approach, and he gave a RailsConf talk about it.
  • Building for edge caching from the start mattered, he said. Retrofitting it later would have been "ten times tougher."

In 2021, he told Indie Hackers that Postgres is "the only technology in the stack that is really precious." He also said the team did not get too enamored with static site generators.

As always, treat those numbers as what the team said at the time. They may not match today.

Not everyone is a fan

A ShiftMag piece on the MLH deal collects community concerns: that DEV's content quality has slipped, with repetitive beginner posts, search-driven writing and AI-generated articles crowding out deeper work. Those are outside opinions, not measurements, and the piece notes some of the complaints predate the current AI wave.

I mention this because a fair story about a community should include the people who are not thrilled with it.

↑ Back to contents

Who does what, in plain English

By now you might be wondering how three people with such different skills actually split the work. The founders have described it themselves, so here is that, with dates attached, because titles change.

Founder How the role was described As of Where it came from
Ben Halpern Co-CEO: long-term vision, product decisions, community leadership Nov 2019 Series A announcement
Peter Kim Frank Co-CEO: partnerships, growth, new opportunities Nov 2019 Same announcement
Jess Lee COO: internal operations, hiring plans, team organization, compensation committee Nov 2019 Same announcement
All three "Forem's co-founders" who lead DEV, no individual titles Current About page dev.to/about

I also found an April 2021 archived copy of the About page that still listed Ben and Peter as co-CEOs and Jess as COO. The current page uses only the group description. So I do not claim any current title for any of them.

The self-descriptions fit those titles nicely:

  • Ben calls himself abstract, chaotic and disorganized.
  • Jess is the organized, disciplined one, per Ben. In 2021, Jess also described an open-source community manager, Christina Gorton, who brings community requests to the engineers.
  • Peter calls himself the least technical, and handles strategy, operations and much of the business and legal side.

You can also see the split in public, though that only tells you about public output, not about who worked hardest. Ben writes most of the announcements and product posts under his own name. Jess wrote the progress report, the open-source thank-you and the remote-work post. And Peter's DEV profile is quieter, with more personal side projects and the occasional post for The DEV Team.

↑ Back to contents

Chapter 10: February 18, 2026 🚀

For a long time, the story of DEV is about growth, and openness, and community. Then in February 2026, it gets a new chapter.

On February 18, 2026, Major League Hacking, known for its student hackathons, announced that it had acquired DEV. MLH's own post, Major League Hacking acquires DEV, says it plainly: "Major League Hacking has acquired DEV (dev.to)." The founders posted their own version the same day, signed "PBJ."

A New Chapter: DEV is Joining Forces with Major League Hacking (MLH)
Ben Halpern
Ben Halpern
for The DEV Team
Feb 18

A New Chapter: DEV is Joining Forces with Major League Hacking (MLH)

#news #devto #hackathon #discuss
445 reactions Comments 125 comments
6 min read

A press release carried the same news. ShiftMag wrote its reaction piece two days later.

What the companies confirmed

I am going to keep this section very clean, because it is where rumors love to grow.

DEV is now part of MLH.

DEV's post says "DEV is officially part of the MLH organization." The wording differs between the two sides ("joining forces" in DEV's post, "acquired" in MLH's), and DEV's own post does not use the word acquisition, but MLH's post and the press release do.

Size.

MLH describes DEV as having more than 3 million developers and MLH as reaching more than 1.5 million across nearly 100 countries, for roughly 5 million together. Those are MLH's figures.

The team stays.

DEV's post says "The original team isn't going anywhere" and that CodeNewbie remains a core part of DEV. It promises a revamped Trusted Moderator program and the return of some past community initiatives, which it calls "immediate, community-first improvements," and not sales initiatives.

Forem continues.

The post says MLH and DEV will remain stewards of Forem, that the partnership will clarify the difference between DEV and Forem, and that Forem will be able to operate more independently. It also admits the team does not have the Forem arrangement "entirely worked out," with news promised in "the coming months." MLH's post says something similar: it is working toward a structure that supports Forem's independence.

Ben has a new role.

He wrote that he was "already hard at work in my new role at MLH." The post does not say what the role is.

A livestream.

A Q&A with Ben, Jess, Peter and MLH's leaders was set for February 19, 2026. I did not watch it, so anything said there is outside this article.

What nobody has said (yet)

I looked hard for these and could not find any of them:

  • The price, the structure (cash, stock, both), the closing date, or a valuation. If you see a number for the deal, it is not sourced.
  • Titles, equity or pay for Jess and Peter after the deal, or Ben's exact role.
  • Who owns and governs Forem now.
  • Any change to DEV's domain, pricing, data handling or staffing, beyond the "original team" line.

The community's first reaction

The ShiftMag piece calls it too early to judge. It collects worries (low-effort content, a site that could turn into a marketing channel for hackathon projects) and some optimism that MLH could help if it curates strong engineering writing. Those are the opinions of the people quoted. I am not adding a verdict of my own.

How Jess described it

The most personal account I found is from Jess. In a post titled A year of change and persistence, dated March 31 (no year on the page, but the WeCoded 2026 banner makes 2026 the obvious reading), Jess called the acquisition "a moment of immense pride that also marked a profound transition."

A Year of Change and Persistence
WeCoded 2026: Echoes of Experience 💜
Jess Lee
Jess Lee
Mar 31

A Year of Change and Persistence

#devchallenge #wecoded #career #dei
114 reactions Comments 33 comments
4 min read

They described what changed. For years, Jess, Peter and Ben ran the company as a trio, and their identities were closely tied to it. After the acquisition, Jess went from holding final responsibility for decisions to being one voice in a larger organization, which means "leading through influence rather than direct authority."

The post also covers things beyond the deal: Jess's decision to use they/them pronouns, the climate for women and underrepresented people in tech, a visit to an MLH hackathon for women in computing, and a line I think is worth repeating, that developers "are the architects of the interfaces the world lives in." It is worth reading in full if you care about the people behind DEV and not just the deal.

↑ Back to contents

Where the three are now

This is the part most likely to go stale, so every line has the date I last checked it. I checked the public pages below on November 10, 2026. DEV leaves the year off recent posts, so where I give a year for a post, I inferred it from the page's own last-updated date.

Ben. His DEV profile still says "Co-founder of DEV" and Community Curator. Recent posts include the Meme Monday series and a series called Daily Context, with the latest in October 2026 (profile last updated October 21). Ben said in February that he was already in a new role at MLH. Neither the post nor the profile names it, so I do not either.

Jess. Jess's profile lists them as Founder-in-Residence at Major League Hacking and co-founder at DEV. I did not find a description of what the Founder-in-Residence role involves.

Peter. His profile says he works "across all things partnerships, sales, biz dev at DEV and MLH." He is still posting: a welcome thread and a post for The DEV Team in 2025, and personal projects through 2026, the latest I saw dated October 13.

Ben Halpern

A Canadian software developer who thinks he’s funny.

Jess Lee

Building DEV with everyone here. What do we have if not community?

Peter Kim Frank

Working across all things partnerships, sales, biz dev at DEV and MLH 🤝️

The three together. The About page, last updated November 9, 2026 according to its metadata, still says DEV is led by Forem's co-founders and that DEV "has joined forces with Major League Hacking." So as of that date, all three are presented publicly as still connected to DEV and MLH. What I cannot tell you is who reports to whom, who holds which title, or whether anyone is in an operating or advisory role.

↑ Back to contents

Epilogue: the ten-year promise

Let me end where I told you we would end.

Back in 2018, Ben told the Changelog he had committed to giving the project ten years. In 2021, he said the same thing to Indie Hackers as advice for open-source founders: commit to a ten-year horizon, even through slow years. If you start counting from when dev.to began in 2016, or from when the three went full-time in 2017, ten years lands in 2026 or 2027.

And that is exactly where the story is now. DEV is part of MLH. Ben is still publicly connected to it, and says he is hard at work in a new role. That is my observation, not something any of them said, and I will not stretch it into a prediction.

What the story shows

Here is what I take away, and I tried to tie each point to something the sources actually show.

  1. The audience came first. The Twitter account began around August 2014 and the dev.to domain arrived roughly twenty months later. By the time the site had 69,259 sessions in October 2016, there was already a crowd to invite.
  2. They combined instead of competing for Ben's attention. Per Jess's report, Ben's conflict between a CTO job and dev.to got resolved by putting three people and their resources together.
  3. Titles came late. The founders said in 2019 that they had barely discussed titles before the Series A.
  4. Open source was a choice, and the community showed up. Contributors made real changes, and some got hired.
  5. Funding stayed modest for a long time. Friends and family in 2017, about $950,000 in 2018, an $11.5 million Series A in 2019, with the three keeping a majority of the board.
  6. The revenue they described stayed small and close to the community. Job listings, sponsors, memberships, and later Forem services.

And a thing I want to say plainly: so many separate pieces had to line up for a Twitter account to turn into a company. An audience. A partner willing to take on a conflict of interest. A third co-founder ready to go full-time. And investors who liked an open-source plan. Each of those is documented. What happened in all the years in between is the part only the founders can fully tell, and I did not talk to them.

The timeline, on one page

If you got lost anywhere above, here is everything with a date, in order. "Approximate" means I worked it out from a source's numbers.

Date What happened
About 2013 Ben and Peter begin working together, after meeting on Reddit (from Ben's and Peter's comments)
About Aug 2014 The Practical Dev Twitter account starts (approximate, from the 2017 report)
Dec 27, 2015 Join date shown on Ben's DEV profile, earlier than the domain date below; Ben first used practicaldev.com, which may explain it (my guess)
About Apr 2016 dev.to domain bought (approximate)
About Jul 2016 Jess joins the project (approximate)
Oct 2016 69,259 sessions for the month
Jan 2017 Product Hunt launch (Jan 2 or 3), Peter joins (Jan 3), the three likely combine efforts (my reading of the report)
Apr 2017 Ben cites about 108,000 Twitter followers
Nov 1, 2017 First monthly progress report, 1,203,378 October sessions
Dec 20, 2017 Peter's AMA on DEV
Jan 2018 Sustaining memberships announced
Aug 8, 2018 Codebase goes open source
Oct 2018 Roughly $950k raised (as described later)
Aug 8, 2019 One year of open source
Oct 10, 2019 Team goes fully distributed
Nov 7, 2019 $11.5M Series A led by Mayfield
May 28, 2020 Forem named
Jul 20, 2021 Forem self-host officially supported
Feb 18, 2026 MLH announces it has acquired DEV

The things I still do not know
  • Who came up with "PBJ," and when.
  • Whether "January 2016" in the 2017 report was a typo for 2017. I think so, for the reasons above, but I have no confirmation from the authors.
  • The terms of the 2018 round, the Series A valuation, and any figure for the MLH deal.
  • What Ben, Jess and Peter do at MLH, and how Forem will be structured.
  • Whether the community's worries about content quality play out once MLH's plans take shape. ShiftMag says it is too early to tell, and I agree.

Your turn 🙂


If you have been on DEV a while, when did you first notice the "PBJ" sign-off, and what did you think it meant? And if you were writing a note to the next team that takes this on, what would you tell them to protect?

Tell me in the comments.

articles.title: Bye, live regions. Hello, ariaNotify()
articles.description: In September 2026, ariaNotify() was introduced as a new web API method to replace live regions. We...
articles.body_html:
In September 2026, ariaNotify() was introduced as a new web API method to replace live regions. We are going to learn when we have to use it, which compliance criteria it meets and its benefits.

Hello, ariaNotify() method!! The title might be a clickbait, because we are far from replacing live regions, buuut... I am super excited about this new feature. I have been waiting for it since 2024 when it was announced in the WAI-ARIA 1.3 draft and it finally becomes baseline, in September of this year (2026) having complete support on Chrome, Firefox, Edge and Safari. So, you might be wondering why the hype, let's find out.

What is ariaNotify()? It is a web API's method that was presented as a programmatic way to trigger screen reader announcements. Yes, same thing as live regions, but the main difference is that live regions are attached to a DOM element and to achieve this now we have to inject hidden text into a DOM element where the change lives, therefore it only announces a text when there is a structural modification on the content. On the contrary, ariaNotify() queues the text to be announced by screen readers using JavaScript.

Markup of Live Regions

A summary of how live regions works nowadays. They need a combination of HTML + CSS + JavaScript to work properly.

<!-- an empty DOM element -->
<p role="status"></p>

// Then, injects the upate on the empty DOM element
const region = document.querySelector('[role="status"]')
region.textContent = '3 results'

Roles

  • role="status": it is used for text that are advisory and not important enough to interrupt. It implies aria-live="polite" and aria-atomic="true".
  • role="alert": it is used for important and/or time-sensitive text and it interrupts what the screen reader is currently saying. It implies aria-live="assertive" and aria-atomic="true".
  • role="log": it is used for new entries in order, like a chat or live updates. It implies aria-live="polite".

WAI-ARIA

  • aria-live: it has three values, polite which waits until the user is idle, assertive which interrupts what the user is perceiving, off which indicates that the changes on a region will only be announced when the user focuses on it.
  • aria-atomic: its value can be true which means that the whole region will be announced when any part of it changes, or false which means that only the part of the region that changes is announced, for example, a clock going from 17.33 to 17.34, only the “34” will be announced.
  • aria-busy: it is used on live regions that might be modified to let the user know when they have been modified. Its value can be true which tells the screen reader that it may wait until the changes are finished before announcing them, or false which means that nothing happens and nothing will be announced until the task is finished.
  • aria-relevant: it is an optional attribute of live regions and it is just a suggestion to assistive technologies. Its values can be additions which refers to element nodes that are added to the accessibility tree within the live region, all, which it is a shorthand for additions removals text, removals which refers to any text content within the live region that is removed from the accessibility tree, or text which refers to text content or a text alternative that is added to any descendant in the accessibility tree of the live region.

Markup of ariaNotify() 


element.ariaNotify('Draft saved.', { priority: 'high' })
  1. Host element or document It is the element that will contain the announcement. It could be the Element in the accessibility tree, or the Document.
  2. Method ariaNotify() The method itself. It is called on the host and it contains the announcement and the options.
  3. Announcement 'Draft saved.' Required. It is the announcement text. Without it there is a TypeError.
  4. Options { priority: 'high' } Optional. If it is omitted or a value that is not on the dictionary is being placed, the value by default would be ‘normal’.
  5. Priority priority: 'high' | 'normal' normal, the default, is spoken after what is being spoken; high interrupts it.

Parallels with Live Regions

In Live Region In ariaNotify Parallelism
role="status", aria-live="polite" { priority: 'normal' } (the default) Both are polite regions and wait until the previous announcement has finished before announcing.
role="alert", aria-live="assertive" { priority: 'high' } Both interrupt what is being spoken to announce the latest message.
element.textContent = 'Draft saved.' element.ariaNotify('Draft saved.') The message to be announced.
aria-atomic="true" announcement text aria-atomic makes a whole region announceable when any part of it changes. In live regions it is applicable to the hidden string to announce but in ariaNotify the announcement text is already the argument to announce

Live Region 

<p role="status" aria-live="polite" aria-atomic="true"></p>

<p role="alert" aria-atomic="true"></p>

const polite = document.querySelector('[role="status"]')
const assertive = document.querySelector('[role="alert"]')

polite.textContent = 'Draft saved.'
assertive.textContent = 'Could not save the draft.'

ariaNotify() 

<button type="button" lang="en">Save draft</button>

const element = document.querySelector('button')

element.ariaNotify('Draft saved.')
element.ariaNotify('Could not save the draft.', {
  priority: 'high',
})

In my opinion, the ariaNotify arrived to simplify the knowledge around announcements. In the past, having to communicate the knowledge about live regions was the biggest challenge for accessibility experts so having a method that with a single line of code covered the screen reader announcements without without hardcoding hidden text is refreshing.

Live Regions vs ariaNotify(): Use Cases

In this section, we will learn with use case examples how ariaNotify() simplifies the work and meets the WCAG success criterion to be compliant.

Here you can test the examples

Should I Document or Should I Element?

Neither of the MDN page for ariaNotify() in Document nor the MDN page for ariaNotify() in Element make a clear distinction between whether to attach the ariaNotify method to the Document or to the Element, but we can state that the choice is about the message per se. Based on that, I created the following table to help decide where to attach the method based on semantics and context.

Another thing worth mentioning is that the language of the announcement by default is, it comes from the lang attribute on the html element. If you want a dedicated section of the page to have a different language, set it explicitly.

Situation Where Why
Announcement about connection, a new version, session update, and a total upate Document The announcement is not tied to an action by the user or to an update in a region, but to a global update that improves or modifies the experience.
Announcement about a thing happening in a section of the page. It could be a count, a total updated, a progress bar, etc Element The announcement has a context, a scope
Announcement of something that has been removed from the DOM Document The Element does no longer exists in the DOM, so the announcement should be made from the Document

Reusable and Global Solution for Announcements Using Just ariaNotify()

In my lib of methods, last month I implemented a reusable function to dispatch announcements programmatically using the ariaNotify() method.

  1. A function to check if the native HTML element supports ariaNotify() 
   export const hasAriaNotify = () =>
     typeof Element !== 'undefined' && 'ariaNotify' in Element.prototype
  1. Create a type (if you are using TypeScript) to tell TypeScript the method may exist and what it takes. 
   type Notifier = {
      ariaNotify?: (announcement: string, options?: { priority: Priority }) => void
    }
  1. Then we have to create a notify function 
   export function notify(
      from: Element | Document,
      message: string,
      priority: Priority = 'normal',
    ) {
      const native = hasAriaNotify()
      const send = () => {
        (from as unknown as Notifier).ariaNotify?.(message, { priority })
      }
      if (native) return send()
    }
  • The function has 3 mandatory parameters: from which checks if the method is being attached to an Element or Document, message which is the string of texts to be announced and priority which is the type of announcement that the screen reader should do.
  • If native is true, we are going to attach the method to the Element/Document and dispatch the action.
    1. The reusable function can be used in the following way: 
   notify(bar, 'report.pdf uploaded.')

Screen Readers

Click here to discover how screen readers announce the announcements of ariaNotify method

WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion - Level AA

Success Criterion Explanation
4.1.3 Status Messages (AA) as in Technique ARIA27, the progress should be announced.
3.3.1 Error Identification (A) For example, a failed upload should be announced with high priority

Browser Support

According to MDN, this is the list of browsers that support ariaNotify on their latest update since September 2026. Oldest versions might not support ariaNotify.

  • Chrome version 141
  • Edge version 141
  • Firefox version 150
  • Opera version 125
  • Safari version 27
  • Chrome Android version 141
  • Firefox Android version 150
  • Opera Android version 93
  • Safari on iOS version 27
  • Samsung Browser version 30
  • WebView Android version 141
  • WebView on iOS version 27

Resources

  • https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Document/ariaNotify
  • https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Element/ariaNotify
  • https://w3c.github.io/aria/#ARIANotifyMixin

So far on Troyal, my fictional royalty-tracking API, I've written the product brief, the API design tables, the README and a Getting Started guide.

Recently, I wrote the OpenAPI spec.

My API design tables say what each endpoint does, in plain words. An OpenAPI file says the same thing in a standard format that tools can read. Many real API docs sites are generated from files like this.

I built it one endpoint at a time:

  • GET /works to list works
  • POST /works to create one
  • GET, PATCH and DELETE on /works/{id} to retrieve, update or delete a single work

Each endpoint has its request body, its success response and its errors (400, 401, 404 and 429), matching the troubleshooting table in my Getting Started guide.

The most useful lesson was how strict the format is. YAML depends on spacing, and a few stray spaces were enough to break my file. I only caught it because I tested everything in Swagger Editor, which turns the file into a live, readable page.

Everything is public on GitHub. Next up: the ownership splits and royalty statements, an error codes guide, and a Jira board to track the docs work.

Troyal is fictional. The documentation is real.

articles.title: Napsha: Testing a Claude Skill for Open Inquiry into AI Subjectivity
