articles.description: A TinySA sweep logger, a CC1101 RSSI cross-check, and a diff script that tells you which spikes...
articles.body_html:
A TinySA sweep logger, a CC1101 RSSI cross-check, and a diff script that tells you which spikes belong to your own room.

Two days ago Hackaday ran a write-up of Logan Zarov turning an LG D325 Android phone into a wideband receiver. Root, LineageOS, a modem firmware change that exposes the baseband stream, an antenna wire, and the Bluetooth radio pressed into service as a local oscillator so the thing can hear down into shortwave. A month earlier it was the ESP32's Wi-Fi block coughing up I/Q samples, then an ESP32-C5 pulling analog drone video out of 5 GHz.

The pattern is clear. Every radio chip in the junk drawer has an SDR hiding inside it, waiting for someone patient enough to find the debug path.

The part nobody posts is the boring half. A hacked receiver with an unknown front end, unknown filtering and an oscillator borrowed from a different radio will show you signals. Some of them will be real. Plenty will be its own spurs, the USB hub's switching noise, your monitor's backlight, and the LED driver in the ceiling. Before you trust anything a clever receiver tells you, you need a reference picture of your own bench, taken with an instrument whose behavior is documented.

That reference is cheap to build. Here is the one I would set up before plugging in anything exotic.

The Kit and Why Each Piece Is There

Three pieces of hardware, each with a job.

The reference instrument is a tinySA Ultra [AFFILIATE: tinySA Ultra]. It is a small swept spectrum analyzer with a USB serial console, a documented command set and a calibrated input. Calibrated matters more than sensitive here. You want a tool whose lies are written down.

The second opinion is a CC1101 module [AFFILIATE: CC1101 433 MHz SPI module] wired to an ordinary ESP32-WROOM dev board [AFFILIATE: ESP32-WROOM-32 DevKit]. The CC1101 is a sub-GHz transceiver from TI with a readable RSSI register. It has nothing in common with the tinySA's front end, which is exactly the point. When two unrelated receivers agree a signal exists, it probably does.

The third piece is a 20 dB SMA attenuator [AFFILIATE: SMA 20dB attenuator 2W]. Every spectrum analyzer has a maximum input level, and the cheapest way to kill one is a strong nearby transmitter coupled straight into the port. The attenuator also gives you a trick for spotting fake signals, covered below.

Everything here is receive-only. The CC1101 can transmit; nothing in this build asks it to.

Sweep the Room With the TinySA Over Serial

The tinySA speaks a NanoVNA-style serial console. Plug it in, and on Linux it enumerates as a CDC device, usually /dev/ttyACM0. Commands end with a carriage return, the device echoes the command, prints its output, and finishes with a ch> prompt.

The command that does the work is scan:

scan 430000000 440000000 450 2

That sweeps 430 to 440 MHz in 450 points. The final argument is an output mask; a value of 2 asks for the measured level of each point, one value per line, in dBm. The community TinySA_Python library uses the same call and parses the first whitespace-separated token of each line as the level. It also documents a firmware quirk worth guarding against: some early-2024 builds emit malformed numbers like -:.000000e+01, which the library patches before parsing.

Frequencies for each point are derived from start, stop and point count rather than read back, because the frequencies command reports the last screen sweep and follows the RBW setting, not the point count you asked for.

The logger below takes a burst of sweeps, keeps the per-bin median and per-bin maximum, and writes a baseline CSV. Install pyserial first.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""tsa_baseline.py: record or compare a tinySA spectrum baseline."""
import argparse
import csv
import statistics
import time

import serial


def command(port, line, timeout=30.0):
    port.reset_input_buffer()
    port.write((line + "\r").encode())
    buf = b""
    deadline = time.time() + timeout
    while not buf.endswith(b"ch> ") and time.time() < deadline:
        buf += port.read(port.in_waiting or 1)
    lines = buf.decode(errors="replace").splitlines()
    return [l.strip() for l in lines[1:] if l.strip() and not l.startswith("ch>")]


def parse_level(token):
    token = token.replace("-:.0", "-10.0").replace(":.0", "10.0")
    return float(token)


def sweep(port, start, stop, points):
    rows = command(port, f"scan {start} {stop} {points} 2")
    levels = [parse_level(r.split()[0]) for r in rows]
    step = (stop - start) / (points - 1)
    return [(start + i * step, lvl) for i, lvl in enumerate(levels)]


def record(args, port):
    runs = []
    for n in range(args.sweeps):
        runs.append(sweep(port, args.start, args.stop, args.points))
        print(f"sweep {n + 1}/{args.sweeps} done")
        time.sleep(args.gap)
    with open(args.file, "w", newline="") as fh:
        out = csv.writer(fh)
        out.writerow(["freq_hz", "median_dbm", "max_dbm"])
        for i in range(len(runs[0])):
            levels = [r[i][1] for r in runs]
            out.writerow([int(runs[0][i][0]),
                          round(statistics.median(levels), 1),
                          round(max(levels), 1)])
    print(f"baseline written to {args.file}")


def compare(args, port):
    with open(args.file) as fh:
        base = [(float(r["freq_hz"]), float(r["max_dbm"]))
                for r in csv.DictReader(fh)]
    now = sweep(port, args.start, args.stop, args.points)
    hot = [(f, lvl, lvl - b) for (f, lvl), (_, b) in zip(now, base)
           if lvl - b >= args.margin]
    for f, lvl, delta in hot:
        print(f"{f / 1e6:10.4f} MHz  {lvl:6.1f} dBm  +{delta:4.1f} dB over baseline max")
    if not hot:
        print("nothing above baseline max + margin")


def main():
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    ap.add_argument("mode", choices=["record", "compare"])
    ap.add_argument("--port", default="/dev/ttyACM0")
    ap.add_argument("--start", type=int, default=430_000_000)
    ap.add_argument("--stop", type=int, default=440_000_000)
    ap.add_argument("--points", type=int, default=450)
    ap.add_argument("--sweeps", type=int, default=30)
    ap.add_argument("--gap", type=float, default=2.0)
    ap.add_argument("--margin", type=float, default=6.0)
    ap.add_argument("--file", default="baseline.csv")
    args = ap.parse_args()
    with serial.Serial(args.port, 115200, timeout=0.5) as port:
        print(command(port, "version"))
        record(args, port) if args.mode == "record" else compare(args, port)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Run it like this:

$ pip install pyserial
$ python3 tsa_baseline.py record --sweeps 30 --file bench_433_night.csv
$ python3 tsa_baseline.py compare --file bench_433_night.csv --margin 6

The design choice that matters is comparing against the baseline maximum, not the median. Your room is not quiet. It breathes. A switching supply that wanders in and out every few seconds will show up in some sweeps and not others, and a median-based comparison flags it every time it reappears. Comparing against the worst the room did during the baseline means the script only speaks up when something exceeds the room's own bad behavior by your margin.

Record more than one baseline. Night and day differ. So does "laptop on charger" versus "laptop on battery." Label the files honestly and keep them.

The Attenuator Test for Signals That Aren't There

Swept analyzers built from mixers generate images and spurs, and cheap ones generate more. The tinySA documentation spends real time on this, and the firmware has settings aimed at it. You can also catch a fake signal with nothing but the attenuator and arithmetic.

Take a sweep with the antenna connected directly. Insert the 20 dB attenuator and sweep again. A real external signal drops by 20 dB, give or take the attenuator's tolerance. A spur generated inside the instrument by a strong signal overloading the mixer does something different: intermodulation products fall faster than the signals that create them, so a third-order product drops by roughly three times the attenuation. Internal spurs that come from the analyzer's own oscillators barely move at all.

That gives you a sorting rule:

drops ~20 dB    -> external signal, keep it
drops far more  -> overload product, your front end is lying under load
barely moves    -> internal spur, belongs to the instrument

Run compare against an attenuated baseline and an unattenuated one, and the differences tell you which entries in your hot list are worth chasing. This same test works on the rooted phone, the ESP32 SDR, or any receiver whose filtering you can't see. It's the cheapest calibration move in radio.

A Second Opinion From the CC1101 Registers

A spectrum analyzer gives you the shape. The CC1101 gives you a vote from a completely different signal chain. The goal is a slow RSSI sweep across the same band you baselined, printed as CSV, so you can line it up with the tinySA results.

The register facts come straight from the CC1101 definitions ESPHome ships: the frequency word lives in FREQ2/FREQ1/FREQ0 at 0x0D to 0x0F, RSSI is status register 0x34, VERSION is 0x31, the strobes are SRES 0x30, SCAL 0x33, SRX 0x34, SIDLE 0x36, the read bit is 0x80, burst is 0x40, the crystal is 26 MHz, and the RSSI step is 0.5 dB with a typical offset of 74.

Status registers share addresses with strobes, which trips up everybody once. Reading 0x34 with only the read bit set sends the SRX strobe. You must set read and burst together, 0x34 | 0xC0, to get the RSSI value back.

#include <SPI.h>

const int PIN_CS = 5;     // VSPI defaults on ESP32-WROOM: SCK 18, MISO 19, MOSI 23
const int PIN_MISO = 19;
const double XTAL_HZ = 26e6;

void select() {
  digitalWrite(PIN_CS, LOW);
  while (digitalRead(PIN_MISO)) {}  // CC1101 pulls SO low when its crystal is stable
}
void release() { digitalWrite(PIN_CS, HIGH); }

void strobe(uint8_t cmd) { select(); SPI.transfer(cmd); release(); }

void writeReg(uint8_t addr, uint8_t val) {
  select(); SPI.transfer(addr); SPI.transfer(val); release();
}

uint8_t readStatus(uint8_t addr) {
  select(); SPI.transfer(addr | 0xC0); uint8_t v = SPI.transfer(0); release();
  return v;
}

void tune(double hz) {
  uint32_t word = (uint32_t)((hz * 65536.0) / XTAL_HZ);
  strobe(0x36);                       // SIDLE
  writeReg(0x0D, (word >> 16) & 0xFF);
  writeReg(0x0E, (word >> 8) & 0xFF);
  writeReg(0x0F, word & 0xFF);
  strobe(0x33);                       // SCAL: calibrate synthesizer at the new frequency
  delay(1);
  strobe(0x34);                       // SRX
  delay(3);                           // let RSSI settle
}

float rssiDbm() {
  uint8_t raw = readStatus(0x34);
  float v = (raw >= 128) ? (raw - 256) / 2.0 : raw / 2.0;
  return v - 74.0;
}

void setup() {
  Serial.begin(115200);
  pinMode(PIN_CS, OUTPUT);
  release();
  SPI.begin();
  SPI.beginTransaction(SPISettings(4000000, MSBFIRST, SPI_MODE0));
  strobe(0x30);                       // SRES
  delay(10);
  uint8_t ver = readStatus(0x31);
  Serial.printf("# CC1101 VERSION=0x%02X\n", ver);
  if (ver == 0x00 || ver == 0xFF) Serial.println("# check wiring, SPI is not talking");
  Serial.println("freq_hz,rssi_dbm");
}

void loop() {
  for (double f = 433.05e6; f <= 434.79e6; f += 25e3) {
    tune(f);
    Serial.printf("%.0f,%.1f\n", f, rssiDbm());
  }
  delay(2000);
}

At 433.92 MHz the frequency word works out to 0x10B071, which you will recognize from half the CC1101 configs on GitHub. If your output shows that tuning landing somewhere else, your crystal is not 26 MHz or your arithmetic is off.

Three honest limitations. The reset-default channel filter is roughly 200 kHz wide, so stepping at 25 kHz oversamples and smears narrow carriers across several bins. The 74 dB offset is a typical figure; TI's datasheet lists offsets that shift with data rate, so treat absolute dBm values as approximate and trust the relative shape. And the spin-wait on MISO is how TI's own timing diagram says to wait for chip-ready, but a dead module will hang the loop there forever. Add a timeout before you leave it unattended.

What you want from the CC1101 run is agreement in position and relative height with the tinySA hot list. A carrier the tinySA reports at 433.92 that the CC1101 also sees rising above its floor is real. A tinySA spike the CC1101 never notices, which also failed the attenuator test, belongs to the analyzer.

Reading the Room Like Evidence

Once you have the logs, the work becomes bookkeeping, and bookkeeping is where most RF hobbyists quit. Write down the time, the antenna, the attenuator state, which devices were powered, and where you were standing. A baseline without that metadata is a picture of nothing in particular.

The questions you can answer with this setup are narrower than the internet would like. You can say a signal was present at a frequency, at roughly a level, at a time, seen by two unrelated receivers. You cannot say what device made it or who owns that device. Detection is where an investigation starts, and every honest RF guide says so in some form.

If the measurement side is where you want to go deeper, the RF Inspection for Beginners: TinySA Spectrum Baseline Guide ($45) is the next step after the script above. It covers instrument setup and calibration before interpretation, picking RBW, sweep speed and max-hold for the specific question you are asking, comparing repeated observations, and documenting time, location, equipment and uncertainty so a sweep turns into a record. That last part is exactly what the Python skips.

If the CC1101 half grabbed you, the registers go a long way past FREQ and RSSI. Bandwidth, deviation, data rate and the AGC all change what that RSSI number means. The CC1101 Deep Dive: Register-Level RF Lab Guide ($35) works through registers, modulation, timing, deviation and noise-floor behavior on ESP32 hardware, receive-only, with a bench workflow for comparing presets against measured parameters. It's the natural follow-on once you want the second-opinion receiver tuned for the signal instead of left on reset defaults.

Then Go Play With the Clever Receivers

Now the phone hacks and ESP32 SDRs get interesting, because you have something to measure them against. Point the hacked receiver at the same band, run the same sweep schedule, and compare its hot list to your two references. Every peak it reports that your references can't confirm is a fact about the hacked receiver, its oscillator, its filtering, its firmware. That's a better result than a pretty waterfall. It is a characterization, and characterizations are what turn a clever hack into a usable instrument.

The receiver that impresses you on day one is rarely the one you trust on day thirty. The one you trust is the one whose lies you have already written down.

Sources: Hackaday, "From Phone, To SDR, No Extra Hardware" (Nov 9, 2026); Hackaday ESP32 tag (ESP32-C5 5 GHz drone video, Oct 20, 2026; ESP32 SDR frequency limits, Oct 15, 2026); LC-Linkous/TinySA_Python README; ESPHome cc1101defs.h; TI CC1101 product page.

articles.title: 0.1 + 0.2 Is Not a Bug. It's Arithmetic in a Costume.
articles.description: The first time 0.30000000000000004 showed up on my screen I did what everyone does. I blamed Python....
articles.body_html:
The first time 0.30000000000000004 showed up on my screen I did what everyone does. I blamed Python. Then I blamed my keyboard. Then Python again, louder.

It's not Python. JavaScript prints the same number, and so does nearly every language on your machine, because nearly every language stores decimals the same way: as IEEE 754 doubles, a standard from 1985 that is older than most of the people complaining about it.

Where does the extra 4 come from?

Write one third as a decimal. You can't. You get 0.333 and then the 3s keep going until you run out of patience or paper, and whatever you eventually write down is close to a third but is not a third.

Binary has the same problem with different numbers. 0.1 in binary is 0.0001100110011..., the "0011" repeating forever. A double gives you 53 bits of precision to store that with, so the machine stores the closest value it can fit and moves on.

You can see the stand-in Python actually uses:

from decimal import Decimal
print(Decimal(0.1))

Output:

0.1000000000000000055511151231257827021181583404541015625

That's the 0.1 your computer owns. 0.2 is a different approximation with a different tail. Add the two stand-ins and the errors come along for the ride:

print(0.1 + 0.2)

0.30000000000000004

Nobody made an error in the addition. The addition is exact. It's exact arithmetic performed on inexact numbers, which is a different and much more annoying sentence.

Does it get worse if you keep adding?

Yes, politely.

total = 0.0
for x in [0.1] * 10:
    total += x
print(total)

0.9999999999999999

Ten copies of almost-0.1, added one at a time, each rounding nudging the pile. Amusing footnote: Python 3.12's built-in sum() returns exactly 1.0 for this, because it now uses compensated summation that tracks the lost crumbs. The plain loop doesn't. When a language starts quietly patching around a problem, that's your sign the problem is everywhere.

When should you actually care?

Two situations. The first is equality. 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3 is False, and any code that compares floats with == is a landmine with a countdown you can't read. Compare with a tolerance instead:

import math
print(math.isclose(0.1 + 0.2, 0.3))

True

The second is money, and this one I take personally. I sell a small digital product priced at $7.99 and work out revenue per visitor in a spreadsheet. The spreadsheet runs on the same doubles. At my scale, a floating point error is a ghost worth a ten-thousandth of a cent and I lose no sleep over it. But the fix costs nothing, so the rule in my notebook is absolute: money is counted in integers of the smallest unit, 799 cents, or in Decimal. Never in floats.

Decimal does base-10 arithmetic, the kind money is actually denominated in:

from decimal import Decimal
print(Decimal('0.1') + Decimal('0.2'))

Decimal('0.3')

Note the quotes. Decimal(0.1), no quotes, builds the decimal out of the binary float, and you already saw what that contains. Feeding Decimal a float is mopping the floor with the muddy water. Strings in, exact decimals out.

JavaScript gets no separate treatment here, because there's nothing to treat. Its numbers are the same doubles:

console.log(0.1 + 0.2 === 0.3);

false

Same standard, same costume, same party.

The part nobody puts on the poster

Floats are not a scam. For graphics, physics, machine learning, anything where the input was an approximation to begin with, a double is fast, hardware-supported, and accurate far beyond what the measurement deserved. The honest catch is that Decimal is slower and grumpier to write, and reaching for it everywhere is its own kind of cargo cult. The sin was never using floats. The sin is using them in the two places they're guaranteed to embarrass you: equality checks and cash.

Every senior dev I've watched hit this has the same story shape. The demo worked. The tests worked. Then the system ran a few million operations, the errors held hands, and a total came out one cent or one vote or one millisecond wrong, and somebody got to spend a Friday finding out why.

Where did floating point last bite you? I want the specific version, the one with the Friday in it.

P.S. Everything I write stays free — that part doesn't change. But if this one was worth something to you, you can buy me a coffee ☕ (one-time or monthly, both work). It covers the API credits and hosting behind these experiments — and honestly, it's also the nudge that gets the next one started on the evenings I'd otherwise skip it. — Salam

articles.title: What a Number-Guessing Game Teaches About Binary Search and Vue State
articles.description: A higher-or-lower number game can give misleading hints or attempt counts if the secret and round...
articles.body_html:
A higher-or-lower number game can give misleading hints or attempt counts if the secret and round state change at the wrong time. I'll use a small Vue implementation to show how to keep those updates consistent, then explain why midpoint guesses put a worst-case bound on the number of attempts.

The player chooses a range, submits a number, and gets a high, low, or correct result. There is no computer player performing binary search. The useful connection is that the feedback gives a human player exactly the information needed to shrink a search interval.

Pick One Secret for the Whole Round

The implementation offers upper bounds of 10, 50, 100, and 1,000, always starting at 1. The target generator is deliberately ordinary:

function randomTarget(max) {
  return Math.floor(Math.random() * max) + 1;
}

Multiplying a random value in the interval from zero up to, but not including, one produces a value below max. Taking the floor gives integers from zero through max - 1; adding one moves the range to the numbers the UI promises.

The target must be generated once per round, not once per submission. Otherwise a helpful-looking “too low” message would describe a secret that might no longer exist when the next guess arrives. That destroys the premise of interval narrowing.

The round reset is also a state transition, not just another random assignment:

function newGame() {
  if (typeof window === "undefined") return;
  target.value = randomTarget(maxNum.value);
  currentGuess.value = null;
  guesses.value = [];
  won.value = false;
  feedback.value = "";
  feedbackType.value = "";
}

I like reading this function as a checklist of everything belonging to one round. The secret changes, input clears, history disappears, the win lock resets, and the previous hint goes away together.

Changing the selected range calls this same reset. Keeping two partially different reset implementations would make it easy to carry an old guess history into a new range or leave the submission button disabled after a previous win.

Record the Attempt Before Announcing the Win

The submission function first checks whether the round is already won, rejects an empty or nonnumeric input, and reports numbers outside the selected bounds. Only then does it compare the guess with the secret.

In the successful branch, the guess is appended before the attempt count is used:

if (g === target.value) {
  guesses.value.push({ value: g, dir: "correct" });
  won.value = true;
  feedback.value = t("guessNumber.correct", { n: guesses.value.length });
  feedbackType.value = "correct";
  if (bestScore.value === null || guesses.value.length < bestScore.value) {
    bestScore.value = guesses.value.length;
  }
}

The history is held in a Vue ref, so both the comparison and the stored score read guesses.value.length. More importantly, the successful submission is included before either read. Counting first and appending afterward would underreport every win by one attempt.

Each history item stores both the submitted value and its direction. The template derives its arrow and appearance from that record. I would rather keep that compact structured history than try to reconstruct previous results from translated feedback strings.

The best score is a separate ref, so starting a new round does not erase it. It is not stored in localStorage, and it is not partitioned by range. A one-guess win in the smallest range can therefore remain the best score when the player switches to 1–1,000. Its lifetime is that of the component instance: refreshing the page or unmounting and recreating the component loses the record. It is a convenience, not a normalized measure of skill.

Higher-or-Lower Feedback Defines a Search Interval

Suppose the secret is somewhere from 1 through 100. Guessing 50 and hearing “too low” eliminates everything from 1 through 50, including the number just tried. The remaining candidates are 51 through 100.

Guessing near the middle of the remaining interval keeps the larger of the two possible remaining groups small. Repeating that strategy is binary search performed by the player. It is the same idea used to search a sorted collection, except the game supplies a comparison instead of exposing an array.

For an inclusive interval [low, high], I would choose Math.floor((low + high) / 2). After a “too low” result for g, the next lower bound is g + 1; after “too high,” the next upper bound is g - 1. Excluding the failed guess matters: keeping it as a candidate can make the search repeat a value instead of progressing, especially when only two candidates remain.

For a range containing 100 distinct targets, seven guesses suffice in the worst case with an appropriate midpoint strategy. More generally, a comparison tree with at most k guesses can accommodate up to 2^k - 1 target values: each comparison can finish at its own node or continue into one of two smaller intervals.

The smallest sufficient bound for N targets is therefore Math.ceil(Math.log2(N + 1)). Six guesses cover at most 63 targets; seven cover 127. That explains the seven-guess guarantee for 100 targets without assuming that every guess has only two outcomes: equality ends the search at the current node.

That bound does not mean every game takes seven attempts. The secret might be the first midpoint, and random guesses can occasionally get lucky. Nor does it mean the component calculates a recommended next guess; it only provides feedback and history.

The component also keeps the input bounds at 1 and the selected maximum, not the narrowed interval. Repeating an earlier guess, or guessing something earlier feedback already ruled out, still counts as an attempt. The guarantee depends on the player's strategy; the interface does not enforce it.

This distinction makes the game a useful teaching example. The state machine supplies trustworthy observations, while the search strategy is a separate layer of reasoning. You can explain interval halving without pretending the application contains a solver that is absent from its source.

Browser Games Still Have Initialization and Input Boundaries

The component begins with a deterministic target of 50 and calls newGame() from onMounted. Randomness is deferred until the browser has mounted the page, rather than producing different secrets during server rendering and the browser's first render.

For a casual guessing game, Math.random() is adequate. It is not a cryptographic secret generator, and a target stored in client-side state is not protected from someone inspecting the application. This is not an architecture for competitive play or prize distribution.

There is also a narrower validation gap: the submission logic checks numeric conversion and bounds but does not check Number.isInteger(g). A fractional guess inside the range can be counted as an attempt even though the generated target is always an integer. For example, 50.5 against a secret of 51 produces “too low” and enters the history. The number input's default step can mark that value invalid, but the click handler and Enter handler call submitGuess directly, without a validating form submission. An integer guard before recording history would close that gap; it is not part of the current implementation.

I turned this small state-machine example into a free browser game: Guess the Number Game.

articles.title: I built a true-scale space flight in three.js, from Earth to Andromeda
articles.description: I've been building a browser space flight where everything sits at its real distance. You leave...
articles.body_html:
I've been building a browser space flight where everything sits at its real distance. You leave Earth, pass the planets at their actual positions for today, fly between nearby stars, and end up outside the Milky Way and at Andromeda.

https://howsmallarewe.com/en/?utm_source=devto

I started it because textbook diagrams put the planets right next to each other, and I never had a sense of how big the gaps are.

It's three.js r170 with Vite and no other rendering library. Three parts took most of the work.

One scene from a metre to 2.5 million light-years

The renderer uses logarithmicDepthBuffer. True positions live on the CPU in km as JS doubles. Every frame I subtract the camera position from everything, so the camera always sits at the origin (floating origin) and the GPU only sees camera-relative coordinates.

That wasn't enough on its own. Polygons more than about 1e15 km from the camera still broke up from float precision. So anything farther than 2e10 km, which is outside Neptune's orbit, gets pulled in to that distance along the same direction and scaled down by the same factor. It keeps the same angular size on screen:

const PROXY_KM = 2e10; // beyond Neptune's orbit (4.5e9 km)

for (const n of nodes.values()) {
  const p = n.root.position.subVectors(n.truePos, camPos);
  const d = p.length();
  const f = d > PROXY_KM ? PROXY_KM / d : 1;
  p.multiplyScalar(f);
  n.root.scale.setScalar(f);
}

Stars that depend on where you are

About 110k stars from the HYG catalogue are packed into a binary file at 20 bytes per star (xyz in parsecs, absolute magnitude, RGB). The vertex shader works out the apparent magnitude from the real camera distance every frame and turns it into point size and alpha. From Earth you get the normal night sky. Fly to Sirius and the sky is drawn as it would look from there.

An ultraviolet sky

Press V to swap the whole sky for the new full-sky UV map by Brice Ménard (released with Anthropic, made with Claude Science). A Python script converts the Mollweide image to equirectangular, and the sky sphere samples it by direction through a J2000 galactic rotation. About a third of the map, mostly the galactic plane, is predicted from other wavelengths, per the map's author.

Flight speed is 0.9 times the distance to the nearest surface per second, so the same keys move you kilometres near a planet and light-years between stars. Planet positions come from Astronomy Engine. The Milky Way you see from outside is a model, not a photo.

Feedback I'd like

  1. Right in front of a UV landmark the additive blending blows out to white and you lose the shape. I haven't found a good fix yet.
  2. Frame rate on your GPU, especially laptops and phones (phones get 4K textures instead of 8K).
  3. Anything that looks wrong at the scale transitions, like stars popping or depth fighting.

Credits: UV map by Ménard (CC BY 4.0), planet textures from Solar System Scope (CC BY 4.0), HYG Database v3.5.1 (CC BY-SA 2.5), positions from Astronomy Engine (MIT).

articles.title: Pip: a desktop pet that notices you, not just your words
articles.description: This is a submission for the Presage SmartSpectra SDK Challenge.           What I Built   Pip is a...
articles.body_html:
This is a submission for the Presage SmartSpectra SDK Challenge.

What I Built

Pip is a little octopus who lives in a tide pool in the corner of my desktop. I can talk to it, and it talks back.

Most AI on my desktop works for me, and it only knows what I type or say. Pip is the other half. It notices me: whether I'm smiling or frowning, how often I blink, roughly how fast my heart and breath are going. When I told it "no" with a little smile, it answered: "Funny thing is, you're smiling a little while you say that."

What Pip does:

  • Reacts to your face, even when you're quiet. Smile and hearts pop up. Look surprised and it jumps. Frown and it frowns back. Nod and it nods. Blink and it blinks back. Stare at it long enough and it gets shy.
  • Talks with you. You speak normally; Pip listens, thinks for a moment, and answers out loud with its mouth moving. Every reply starts with a small action (happy, shy, nod, comfort…) that Pip acts out.
  • Hears more than words. Along with what you said, Pip's brain gets a short note of what the camera saw while you said it: expression, blink count, heart and breathing rate, and whether they went up or down.
  • Breathes with you. The water in its pool rises and falls with your chest, and it glows faintly with each heartbeat.

It's a pet, not a tool. It can't open files, read the page I'm on, or browse, and that's on purpose. Agents that read your screen and use your computer already exist, and I didn't want to build yet another harness that I'd never use. I built the one piece I hadn't seen: an agent that can read the person in front of it. The idea is that this piece could later plug into other desktop pets and agents, rather than living only inside Pip. So this is a small demo of that one ability.

The octopus is just one look. The sensing doesn't care what the pet is: a fish, a cat, a little robot, whatever you like. Any of them gets the same new senses, your expressions, your heartbeat, your breathing, and can respond to them in its own way. What I'm really adding is more ways for desktop AI to perceive the person; Pip is one way to show it.

Demo

In the video I'm reading DEV. Pip can't see the page; it only sees me. I react to the posts, and Pip reacts to me. A few things it said, unscripted:

  • "Hello hello! You look a bit surprised to see me."
  • "I'm good, just bobbing about in my pool. You're blinking a lot though."
  • "Funny thing is, you're smiling a little while you say that."
  • "I can chat, keep you company, and sometimes notice things like a smile or a frown. I can't use your computer or look stuff up yet though."

It isn't perfect: a couple of times it didn't catch what I said, and once it told me my message got cut off. Heartbeat and breathing are there (the glow and the water) but subtle on screen.

Code

wenwei-lin / tidepal

Tidepal

Pip is a desktop pet that notices you, not just your words: a little octopus who lives in a tide pool on your desktop. You can talk to it.

Voice assistants only hear your words. Pip also sees how you look while you say them: it uses the SmartSpectra SDK to read your face, blinks, breathing and heartbeat through an ordinary webcam, and passes that along with what you said. So when you say "I'm fine" with a frown, Pip can notice.

  • Talk — speak normally. Pip listens (the ring around the pool follows your voice), thinks, and answers out loud, moving its mouth.
  • Face — Pip blinks when you blink, blushes when you smile, jumps when you look surprised, nods along when you nod, and gets shy if you stare.
  • Breath — the water in Pip's pool rises and falls with your chest; Pip glows with your heartbeat.
  • …
View on GitHub

Electron app. Setup is in the README: npm install, put your keys in .env, npm start.

How It Responds to Human Signals

The SmartSpectra Node SDK runs inside the Electron renderer and reads the webcam on the device. I request the breathing, cardio and face metric groups and decode the protobuf stream.

Signal What Pip does
Expressions (happy, surprise, sad, angry) Mirrors you in real time; tells the chat model how you looked while speaking
Blinking Blinks back; blink count goes to the chat model
Talking Tilts its head and listens
Face landmarks Eyes follow you; nod and shake detection; the "stare" reaction
Breathing trace and rate The water level; rate and trend go to the chat model
Pulse trace and rate The heartbeat glow; rate and trend go to the chat model (stable readings only)

The conversation loop:

camera ─► SmartSpectra (on device) ─► face, blinks, heart, breathing ─┐
                                                                      ├─► DeepSeek V4.1 Flash ─► reply + action tag
mic ─► cut at pauses ─► speech-to-text (SenseVoice) ─► your words ────┘              │
                                                       Pip acts out the tag, macOS speaks the reply

Things I learned on the way:

  • The chest matters. Breathing needs your shoulders and chest in view, which fights with how close we sit to a laptop. Expressions and pulse come through fine from the face alone, so Pip leans on those and only nags about the chest when it really needs breathing.
  • Raw breathing is jumpy. Drawn as-is, the water jerked up and down. I remove the slow drift, let the size of the swing adapt over a few seconds, and move the water with a soft spring. Now it glides.
  • "Face present" should come from expressions. Landmarks sometimes stop while the SDK waits for a better view; expression scores keep coming, so I count those as "I can see you."
  • Only stable numbers. Heart rate jumps around for the first seconds. Pip shows "measuring" until the SDK marks the reading stable, and only stable readings reach the chat model.

Prize Categories

Most Creative or Delightful Use.

Consent and Data Handling

  • Consent. On first launch Pip explains, in plain words, what the camera and microphone are for, and asks. "Just looking" never turns either on. A button turns the camera off any time. A small mirror shows exactly what the camera sees.
  • Video stays on the computer. The SmartSpectra SDK processes frames locally. Nothing is recorded, saved or uploaded. The SDK contacts Presage only to check the key and download its models.
  • SDK telemetry is off (enableTelemetry: false).
  • Voice. When you pause, the piece you just said is sent to a speech-to-text service (SiliconFlow SenseVoice) and turned into text. Audio is not saved. The mic is ignored while Pip is thinking or speaking.
  • AI service. Your words, plus a one-line description of what the camera saw (for example "face while speaking: frowning; heart rate about 81/min, faster than earlier"), go to DeepSeek V4.1 Flash to write Pip's reply. Nothing else is sent.
  • Retention. The conversation lives in memory and is gone when you quit. Only your consent choice and language are saved locally.
  • Not medical. Pip is told never to diagnose or interpret your numbers, and to say it's just a little octopus if you ask about health.

What's next

Pip is a pet on purpose. But the same "eyes for the person" could sit next to other agents:

  • Coding agents. Codex already has desktop pets: little companions that float over your windows and react to what the agent is doing, "thinking" or "task done". They look at the work. A pet with Pip's eyes could also look at the person: notice you frowning at a diff, or grinning when the tests pass, and respond to that. Coding agents like Codex or Claude Code already have the computer and the web; add how you're doing, and an agent could slow down and explain more when you look lost. I don't know of anyone doing this yet, and it seems like a fun interaction to try.
  • Speaking practice. When you practise a language or a talk, the moments you frown or hesitate are the parts you haven't figured out yet. Pip could mark them and go over them with you afterwards.
  • Coaching. A coach could get a small timeline of your expressions next to the transcript, to see which questions landed and which didn't.
  • Calm moments. A short breathing break where the tide follows your breath. I built a version of this and set it aside for now.

articles.title: The Little Markdown Builder Behind My Kids' Element Name Guides
articles.description: Elemon is a periodic table card game I made for my sons. Every element is a card and every move is a...
articles.body_html:
Elemon is a periodic table card game I made for my sons. Every element is a card and every move is a true fact. Over time the site grew a /learn/ section with guides for kids and parents: all 118 element names, why gold is Au, how to teach element names in elementary school, that kind of thing.

Those guides are plain Markdown in content/learn/*.md. One Node script, tools/build-learn.mjs, turns them into static HTML. No framework, and the pages need no JavaScript to read. This post is about the parts of that script I'd build again.

Front matter that errors loudly

Each guide starts with a small front matter block. Here's the one for the gold page:

slug: why-is-gold-au-element-symbols-that-dont-match
title: Why Is Gold Au? 11 Odd Element Symbols, for Kids
h1: Why is gold Au? The 11 element symbols that don't match their names
description: Why is gold Au and iron Fe? A kid-friendly guide to ...
short: The old Latin and German names hiding behind Na, K, Fe, ...
published: 2026-11-09
modified: 2026-11-09
byline: dad
toc: none
faq: A few more questions
cards: Na, K, Fe, Au
hero_element: gold

The parser is about a dozen lines. It splits on the --- fences and reads key: value pairs. The checks after it are where the value is. A guide with no slug, title, h1, description, short, published or modified date fails the build. So does a title over 62 characters, a description outside 140 to 162 characters, or the word "free" anywhere in a title. Search engines cut long titles off, and I'd rather find out at build time.

The names table can't have a gap

The element names guide has a table of all 118 elements with a say-it spelling and what each name comes from. I didn't want 118 rows of hand-written HTML, so the data lives in content/element-names.json:

{
  "H": ["HY-druh-jun", "Greek words for *water-maker*: burn it and you get water"],
  "He": ["HEE-lee-um", "*Helios*, the Greek word for the Sun, where it was spotted first"]
}

A {{element-names}} placeholder in the Markdown expands into the full table. The builder walks the same element list the game uses, sorted by atomic number, and if any symbol is missing from the JSON it throws. That one check is why I trust the table. A typo in a key stops the build, so the live table never ships with a hole in it.

Symbol origins get the same treatment. Gold's row says "an old English word; Au is from Latin aurum." Lead's says Pb is from Latin plumbum. Tungsten's says W is from German Wolfram. Each name row links to that element's card, so a kid who reads "Au is from aurum" is one click from the gold card.

The header card is the real card

I wanted each guide to open with an actual Elemon card instead of stock art. So hero_element: gold (a symbol or a name both work) puts gold's card in the page header.

The trick is that the builder doesn't have its own copy of the card. It loads the browser files the game already ships, data.js, facts.js, types.js, holo.js and dex-show.js, into a Node vm context and calls the same face() function the Elemondex uses:

const ctx = { window: {} };
vm.runInNewContext(readFileSync(`${root}site/js/data.js`, "utf8"), ctx);
for (const f of ["facts.js", "types.js", "holo.js", "dex-show.js"])
  vm.runInNewContext(readFileSync(`${root}site/js/${f}`, "utf8"), ctx);
const SHOW = ctx.window.ElemonShow;

The front of the header card is that face. The back shows the element's number, symbol, family, type and three facts from facts.js. A small script adds the tilt and lets kids drag or tap to turn it over. When I change a card in the game, every guide that uses it picks up the change on the next build. A hero element that isn't a real element throws, and so does a page that doesn't open with a paragraph, because the card sits next to that opening answer.

Old #links keep working

Most of these guides have been rewritten at least once, and headings changed. Old links like #five-activities could already be sitting in someone's notes or a class handout, and I didn't want them landing at the top of the page.

Two things handle it. A heading can pin its id with ## Heading text {#some-id}, so I can reword the heading and keep the anchor. For headings that got renamed or removed, content/learn-anchors.json maps old ids to new ones, or to null when the section is gone:

"best-periodic-table-games-for-kids": {
  "how-did-i-pick-these-games": "how-i-picked-them",
  "the-quick-comparison": null
}

The builder drops an empty <span id="old-id"> right before the heading it moved to, or before the first section when there's nowhere better. Right now that file covers 112 old ids across 16 guides.

Fewer template tells

I wanted the guides to read like someone wrote them, so most of the extra blocks are opt-in per page. A table of contents only shows up by default on pages with five or more H2s. FAQ schema only exists if the page has the heading named in faq:, so there's no identical FAQ box stapled to the bottom of everything. Even the "When you're ready" line at the end of the parent guides rotates its links based on a hash of the slug, so two pages next to each other don't end the same way.

The hub has one rule of its own. Every guide has to be placed in exactly one section, and the script throws if a guide is missing or listed twice. With a new kids' story planned every other day, that catches the "forgot to add it to the hub" mistake before it ships.

If you want to see the output, the gold page lives under elemon.win/learn/. Drag the card in the header.

articles.title: I fed one tarball to 8 tar readers and got 5 different folders
articles.description: The file is 4,096 bytes. Eight blocks of 512.  I extracted it with the tar that ships on my Mac, and...
articles.body_html:
The file is 4,096 bytes. Eight blocks of 512.

I extracted it with the tar that ships on my Mac, and a two-byte file came out 512 bytes long. Its first eight characters spell smuggled.

The archive comes from Harmen Stoppels, who wrote up The Hardest Tarball? last week and collects cases like it in a test suite called tar-minefield. I ran his case through every tar reader I had on hand. None of them crashed. They just disagreed.

What's inside the 4 KB

The case is F35 in the suite, and its page on the project site lays out every block. In order:

  1. A regular file a holding a\n.
  2. A pax extended header with one record: size=512.
  3. A hardlink h pointing at a. Its own header says size 0, but the pax record before it says 512.
  4. A header for an empty file named smuggled.
  5. The two zero blocks that end the archive.

So the whole fight is over block 4. If a hardlink can carry data, those 512 bytes belong to h. If it can't, they're the header of a third file. POSIX says data for a hardlink "may be included" (Stoppels quotes that line in his post), and stops there. It doesn't say what the data should do.

His post builds a cousin of this archive with a single GNU tar command. I don't have GNU tar on this Mac, so I used the suite's own file and checked it against the hash on the case page: 9cda45a9...07760, a match.

Eight readers, one Mac

Each reader got its own empty folder. For Python I used tarfile with filter="data", the mode the project's matrix lists for pip. For Go I wrote a 39-line extractor on top of the standard archive/tar reader, so the framing is Go's and the file writing is mine. node-tar and tar-fs went into a throwaway folder through npm. The rest were already installed.

Here's what landed on disk:

reader                      a       h          smuggled
macOS tar (bsdtar 3.5.3)    512 B   512 B      -
Python tarfile 3.15.2       2 B     2 B        0 B
Perl Archive::Tar 2.38      2 B     2 B        0 B
Go archive/tar 1.23.5       2 B     2 B        0 B
node-tar 7.5.22             2 B     2 B        -
tar-fs 3.1.3                2 B     2 B        -
PHP PharData 8.5.12         2 B     0 B (*)    0 B
RubyGems 4.0.3              2 B     -          0 B

(*) PHP made h a separate empty file, not a link.

Five different trees. The macOS one is the strangest, so I looked inside:

$ xxd x-bsdtar/a | head -1
00000000: 736d 7567 676c 6564 0000 0000 0000 0000  smuggled........
$ cmp <(dd if=F35.tar bs=512 skip=5 count=1 2>/dev/null) x-bsdtar/a && echo same
same

bsdtar took the pax size at its word, read the next 512 bytes as the hardlink's content, and wrote them through the link. Since h and a are one file, the original a\n is gone. In its place: the header block of a file that, for bsdtar, never existed.

One detail surprised me more than the table. Python and Go both report h with a size of 512. Then they read the very next block as a header anyway. They see the claim and set it aside.

My results match the site's matrix for the readers we share, though my bsdtar (3.5.3), Perl module (2.38) and RubyGems (4.0.3) are older than the versions listed there. Go is the exception: the site tests containerd's extractor, and I used the bare standard library. The site has 24 rows for this case, and four reject it outright: .NET's System.Formats.Tar, Julia's Tar.jl, uv's tar-codec, and live-bootstrap's untar (unless it's run with --non-strict).

The bug lives between two readers

Here's the claim I want to make. Most of these readers aren't broken in a way you could file a clean bug about. Each picks a reading of a loose spec, and most of the readings are defensible. The danger shows up when two of them sit in the same pipeline.

Picture an upload service that scans archives with Python's tarfile, hashes each member, and approves the bundle. Then a build step on a Mac unpacks it with the system tar. The scanner approved an a holding two bytes. The disk has 512 bytes it never hashed. Flip the pair and a node-based tool never sees smuggled, while a Python installer writes it.

The project README names exactly this: a scanner and an extractor built on different implementations can be looking at different files. Its catalogue of ambiguities also files this case's family next to real advisories for tokio-tar, tar-rs and node-tar.

So the question for your own stack isn't "is my tar library correct?" It's "do all the places that read this archive agree?"

Strict is cheaper than it sounds

Stoppels thinks rejecting is the best outcome, even if it bends POSIX. Not everyone in the HN thread agreed. One commenter (molticrystal) said they'd always rather get something out of a damaged archive than nothing. Another (rwmj) suggested two modes: refuse anything odd from untrusted uploads, salvage what you can from your own corrupted backup. A third (stabbles) described tar as a format with two jobs, backup and software distribution, that want opposite threat models.

That split feels right to me. If you're installing software or accepting uploads, reject. And the cost is measured, not guessed. The case page says this shape turned up in none of the 82,586 release tarballs scanned from Spack, nixpkgs, Guix, PyPI, crates.io, RubyGems and live-bootstrap. The README says the project's whole default policy still accepts 99.80% of them.

Check your own pipeline today

The suite ships a checker that takes any extract command. The README shows it like this:

python -I suite/check.py -- tar -xf '{archive}' -C '{dest}'

I didn't run it. It's code from a clone, and for a post I only run my own scripts. I read it instead: it extracts each case into its own temp folder and flags anything written outside it.

What I did run is a stopgap for this one case, in eleven lines:

import sys, tarfile

def check(path):
    with tarfile.open(path) as t:
        for m in t.getmembers():
            if (m.islnk() or m.issym()) and m.size:
                return f"reject: {m.name!r} is a link that claims {m.size} bytes of data"
    return "ok"

for p in sys.argv[1:]:
    print(f"{p}: {check(p)}")

in/F35.tar: reject: 'h' is a link that claims 512 bytes of data
in-own/clean.tar: ok
in-npm/tar-7.5.22.tgz: ok
in-npm/tar-fs-3.1.3.tgz: ok

clean.tar is one I made with macOS tar from a file, a hardlink to it and an empty file. It works because Python reports the 512 even while ignoring it. It's a tripwire for one of the suite's 134 cases, not a policy. For real coverage, run the checker, or put a strict reader at the front of the pipeline.

Rough edges

This is a working draft, and it says so: verdicts carry a "draft" label, and new cases are still landing (an open PR adds 54). The repo is heavy, about 127 MB by GitHub's count. My shallow clone stalled, so I pulled the files I needed through the API. I also couldn't test GNU tar, BusyBox, 7-Zip, Java, .NET, Rust or Julia here; for those, the numbers above are the site's, not mine.

Which tar reader unpacks things in your deploy path, and is it the same one your scanner uses?
